251.t: Road conditions: mud roads, pushing the bus
251.s: Long jumps over unpaved roads, rocks under the wheels, the hot motor in Virginia mountains, running out of money.
251.q: Only work. Everybody knew where he rocked with flanks, so he run right to the rocks. Yeah. Couldn't waste the time, because it's grown on. And it gets it all the way.

251.t: Receiving mail on the road via general delivery
251.s: The band had no headquarters; mail went by general delivery and Albert's wife collected it.
251.q: and start to get away. Whatever. I think you've gotten that touch with somebody. Got to take it with me because at that time you say you need a truck in your eye. I got Willis, Willis out of the band, I was with you. Somebody called me. I think you got in touch with me.

251.t: Band books, trunks, valets and travelling party
251.s: Each man had his own book, kept in one big trunk at night. As many as 21 travelled including wives, with bus driver Wilbur Usand and Luther handling setup; musicians cared for their own clothes and music.
251.ch: Running the band on the road
251.q: Well, each musician had his own book. However, at the end of the, the conclusion of the performance at night, we would put them all in one big trunk that we had. And we had the guys that would drive the bus and you, well, the regular maintenance man, we call them, and valets, and they would take…

251.t: Touring the Northeast and the weather
251.s: They played all over, including upstate New York, Vermont and Albany; Allen asks about weather and Canada.
251.q: Well, we're up to Grand Falls, New York. Way upstate. Yeah. In Albany. But we didn't go out there. But we didn't go out there. Yeah. No, no. We stayed there.

251.t: Arriving early, dressing and tailor-made uniforms
251.s: They reached towns in the morning, dressed in private homes and rarely had dressing rooms. Albert's band was among the best dressed, with matching suits from the Texas tailor Goldberg for about sixty dollars.
251.ch: Running the band on the road
251.q: Well, most of the times we always got in town early in the morning and gave us time to find a place to rest and clean up and get ready about 8, 8, 8.30 at night and go right to the dance halls. And when we finished that night, if the next jump was 150, 200, 300 miles, we'd leave right after the…

251.s: A flash flood in Virginia; the band never went west to Albuquerque.
251.q: What about, did you ever run into any flash floods? Yeah, it was large, yeah, it was large, sons. Uh, one time in, uh, Virginia, I can't remember the name of the place. Yeah, they're ready.

251.t: Road hardships: the Natchez dance hall fire, cold, mosquitoes
251.s: Albert escaped a job at a hall that later burned, recalls playing in the cold and under mosquito netting at Port Arthur, and says Lloyd Glenn kept a book of nightly takings.
251.ch: Later years and the Texas scene
251.q: Unfortunately, that never happened too often. Just one time, I think that I can remember, when Walter Barnes did the job in the place where they were burned. I ran in Natchez. Well, I was supposed to play that job. But instead I was playing in another little town. I can't call the name of the town,…

251.t: First travels and crossing Lake Pontchartrain
251.s: Albert says poor family meant no travel until he played music, when a boat trip across Lake Pontchartrain seemed a great journey.
251.q: Yeah. No. I never was able to travel. My people were poor people. And we didn't have any money traveling. Well, I didn't start to travel until I learned how to play. And I was playing on the Sesquahanna and I thought that was the longest trip that I could ever make. Crossing Lake Punch and Train…

99.t: Snow, flat tires and failed dates through Nashville and Georgetown
99.s: Bad weather cancels the Nashville dance and a flat tire makes them miss Georgetown, leaving Charles to give up his suitcase to pay a lodging bill.
99.q: We stayed around Memphis a few weeks. And we got ourselves together on our way back to Cincinnati, Ohio. We get in the two cars and left Memphis on our way to Nashville, Tennessee to play a dance. We ran into a big snow, we get to Nashville, the dance was called off, on account of bad weather. So…

99.t: Racing to Memphis for New Year's Eve at the Casino Ballroom
99.s: After a hotel job in Oklahoma City, the band drives all night, breaks down at Cabot, and reaches Memphis after midnight.
99.q: Oklahoma City we played about Oklahoma City until the latter part of the year, the next to the last day in the year we had a big job to play at one of the big hotels there in Oklahoma City and we played this job and we were booked the following night, which was New Year's evenight in Memphis,…

99.t: New England tour with Roberts and the end of Trent's band in Albany
99.s: Roberts of Pittsfield books them through the Berkshires, Maine and New Brunswick until Trent's band disbands in Albany.
99.q: Out of Mr. Roberts. A fellow named Roberts out of Pittsfield, Mass., hired our band. And we played all through the Berkshires of Massachusetts, we played down on the Cape, we played through the Adirondacks, he kept us pretty busy.

99.t: Scarpelli's promise and the 1934 heat wave tour
99.s: Scarpelli guarantees them the Club Plantation in the fall; on tour in Kansas, Walter Page collapses in 107 degree heat and they see the Dust Bowl.
99.q: That's right, that's what he did. He said if we wanted to go back to Cleveland, he would pay our way back to cleveland. He said if we want to stick around and take this tour and keep your band together, he would put us in the Club Plantation that FALL. That's what he did.

99.t: Booked into a pocket in Syracuse, 1930
99.s: They drive east on borrowed money to a Syracuse job that does not exist; part of the band breaks up and survivors earn small roadhouse and New York State dates.
99.q: And we scuffled and scuffled and scuffled and made our way down back into Texas. And I can remember a booking agent contacting us in Texas, and promised us a big job up in Syracuse, New York. We got together and saved what little money we could to get enough gasoline to get us back out East.

99.t: Gingham Inn, Jean Calloway and re-forming the band for a tour
99.s: After the Gingham Inn closes, owners bring in singer Jean Calloway; Hudson, Walter Page, Morty Long, Lester Nichols and Trombone Smitty join as the band tours.
99.q: Gingham Inn, yes. We played about three and a half -- about three weeks. And they closed -- and the place closed down. So the owners decided to keep our band do -- together, they secured the services of a young lady named Jean Calloway. Jean Calloway had a nice voice and she could front a band. And…

99.t: Leaving home for Johnnie Brown's Playtone Orchestra in Mississippi
99.s: Toe Morgan brings him to Jackson, Tennessee, where he joins Johnnie Brown's orchestra and tours Mississippi towns, the delta, and sees the Shiloh battlefield.
99.q: And this same -- a buddy of mine, the fellow who got me that first job I told you about, "Toe" Morgan. His name was James "Toe" Morgan. He had a job in Jackson, Tennessee, and asked me did I want to go over to Jackson, Tennessee, and join the Johnnie Brown's orchestra. Johnnie Brown and his…

99.t: Stranded by a booker in Jackson, Mississippi, over New Year's 1939
99.s: A broke promoter books the band in Mississippi on nerve; a country club New Year's Eve job pays their bills and gets them home.
99.q: : She sure did. Because the band toured -- the band came out of the Plantation during the holidays, And we went to Arkansas and all down through Mississippi. And they booked us down in Jackson, Mississippi. And we like NOT got out of Jackson, Mississippi.

124.t: Months of travel with Chick Webb's band
124.s: They toured south to Florida, then back through Cincinnati, Chicago and out west for six months straight.
124.ch: Depression gigs, Lil Armstrong, joining Chick Webb
124.q: We gigged. We would go to Baltimore, Washington, Hampton -- on the beach down there, to play the school, you know. We go on down to Atlanta, Charleston, all around. We played all the way down to Florida.

124.t: Ella arriving in Savannah after a day on the bus
124.s: Ella had to dress on the bus before greeting crowds of girls; one-nighters were especially hard on a woman traveling.
124.ch: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
124.q: I know when we get in Savannah, the bus came in and went down and come around and circled the main street of the colored neighborhood. And everybody was standing with their little girls waiting to meet Ella Fitzgerald, you know.

124.t: Travelling by bus with Chick Webb
124.s: The band travelled in one bus, overloaded with baggage, and played big dates like the twelve thousand crowd in Kansas City.
124.ch: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
124.q: Equipment and the extra clothes and the baggage. We got stopped coming out of St. Louis for that. We had too much. We had came through -- we were in Florida for awhile. I'll never forget that. We had all -- Remember I tell you the time with Chick (inaudible) St. Louis and we were going to Kansas…

124.t: Lunceford's Midwest and East dates, then the Audubon
124.s: Over two months McRae travelled with Lunceford through the Midwest, then played the Audubon, Trenton and Washington.
124.ch: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
124.q: up that night because the band had been on the road so long, you know. They came in from Buffalo and all the wives met the band (inaudible) and everything.

124.t: Buses, drivers and the route through the states
124.s: Moe Gale rented a Greyhound-type bus; they played all the main towns on the way west.
124.ch: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
124.q: We had a driver that came with the bus, you know, from the company. We used to rent those Greyhound buses. We used to get seconds, you know. Like you can buy buses (inaudible). They had these buses -- This particular trip with Chick we had been using this bus on previous years, you know. So this…

124.t: Dressing on the bus and playing two sets without the books
124.s: The band changed on the bus, valets set up the stand, and head arrangements like "St. Louis Blues" opened sets.
124.ch: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
124.q: They would set up the bandstand while we be getting dressed. We'd walk right out. They'd take all the instruments and set them up on the stands,

124.s: McRae lists the road manager and valets, buying suits at Young and Taylor, and the clothes changes with Chick versus Cab Calloway.
124.ch: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
124.q: We were responsible for -- No. That -- I was responsible for everything in a way, but with that we gave to -- we had like two --

124.t: The band's trick to rent a hotel cheaply
124.s: The musicians parked the bus away and checked in a few at a time, renting the whole hotel before the owner knew.
124.ch: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
124.q: hotel. So we would go park the bus like two blocks down around the corner where nobody in that neighborhood would know that we were in town.

78.t: One-nighters out of Chicago: Missouri, Kansas City and St. Louis booking
78.s: After long residencies the band took month-long breaks, with a band secretary writing promoters in Kansas City and St. Louis to chain one-nighters around Joplin and Missouri.
78.ch: Touring, recording and Fletcher's band in the 1940s
78.q: Well yes. We did a few one-nighters. We went down in Missouri. You know, after having played on the job for a long time, sometimes the boss would want you to go out for a month, and, you know, he said take a little vacation and when you come back, you won't be stale to yourself, one of those…

78.t: Physical hazards of bus travel before the freeways
78.s: Slow roads and poorly cushioned buses meant 500-mile hauls, hamburgers and arriving just in time to wash and dress, though a big enthusiastic crowd made you forget it.
78.ch: Clubs, publishers, unions and life in Denver
78.q: Well, I would say a lot of times it was a physical hazard, because of the fact that, as you mentioned before, we didn't have the highways that we have now, freeways and whatnot. It took you twice as long to get to your destination, you know, and sometimes riding in even the older buses that the…

78.t: The Newark Charter Company buses that New York bands rented
78.s: Most New York bands used Newark Charter Company's cheap per-mile buses with instruments at the back and bags on top; Fletcher and Horace never owned one.
78.ch: Clubs, publishers, unions and life in Denver
78.q: No, I tell you, there was a certain bus company that most of the bands that traveled out of New York City used. It was called the Newark Charter Company, and I think the reason for that is because their rate by the mile was so much lower than the Greyhound or the Santa Fe, one of those things, and…

78.t: Overnight stays, departure times and musicians who missed Fletcher's bus
78.s: Distance decided whether bands stayed overnight; Fletcher gave a half-hour grace before leaving, and some men hired a car after oversleeping.
78.ch: Clubs, publishers, unions and life in Denver
78.q: Well, that would depend upon the distance of the next engagement. Like if you'd play a place tonight, like say Jacksonville, Florida, and you only had 200 miles to go. Well then, you'd stay all night in Jacksonville after you'd finished the date, which was a welcome sight, a welcome relief, we'll…

78.t: Ivory Joe Hunter's equipped bus and Nat Towles charging rent
78.s: Ivory Joe Hunter bought a specially equipped bus from his royalties, and Nat Towles charged his players $35 a month to sleep on his bus.
78.ch: Clubs, publishers, unions and life in Denver
78.q: Well, he was a smart guy, man. He bought a bus for his band. Well, he got so many royalties, so much money from the tunes that he had written, of course, he had a lot of hits, and, man, he bought a bus that was quite expensive, and I had the pleasure of going through that bus, and he showed it to…

78.t: Life on the road in Fletcher's band: bachelors, nightly pay and percentages
78.s: Fletcher's men liked travel, joked about becoming bachelors, and earned a nightly salary on one-nighters; weekly pay and percentage deals are compared.
78.ch: Fletcher as a leader and early bandmates
78.q: Yes. Oh, I see. Well, I'll tell you, I think the fellows in Fletcher's band liked to travel because of, number one, a lot of the guys were single, and a lot of the guys that weren't single traveled so long that they became single.

78.t: North Carolina warehouse dance and fan mail from WBBM
78.s: In North Carolina the band played a mixed audience in a warehouse with a portable floor and the bus inside. Horace weighed fan mail from the powerful WBBM to choose one-nighter routes.
78.ch: Touring, recording and Fletcher's band in the 1940s
78.q: (Unaudible) and this was a mixed audience, and we would drive the bus -- we had a bus at that time that we could rent, you know, and we could drive the bus right up into the warehouse, you know, right next to the --

176.t: De De's band travels: Paul Barnes, Nellie Lutcher, Texas, and sitting in with Bunk
176.s: De De describes leaving with Paul Barnes and organizing a seven-piece band touring Louisiana and Texas, Nellie Lutcher as pianist, and sitting in with Bunk.
176.ch: De De's career and trumpet players
176.q: I'm telling you about myself. Well I left here with Paul Barnes. I think he's still playing. He's in Chicago now. He left here. Me and his brother. We formed a band and we traveled. Yeah, he was all signed. I got a card. Yeah, he got a card for him. And then we organized a seven piece band. Well…

176.t: Timeline and touring Alabama towns alone
176.s: She dates leaving Pensacola and first coming to New Orleans around 1929 and lists the Alabama towns she played solo.
176.ch: Touring Alabama and Florida, first New Orleans trips
176.q: Yeah, people come in and go and get their liquor and drinks and dance, gamble, you know, all that, the gambling thing like that. Oh yeah. And let's see, when did you say you left Pensacola? I left Pensacola, let's see, we married 35, how did he? How much of Michigan, I tell you, 27, 28. I came to…

176.t: Back in Pensacola with Mac: Florida tours and personnel
176.s: After a year in Birmingham Billie toured Florida towns with Mac's six-piece band, including a Christmas back-and-forth run.
176.ch: Touring Alabama and Florida, first New Orleans trips
176.q: Then I, uh, went home. Going to Pensacola. Went to Pensacola. You played solo there, or you worked with bands? I worked with bands. That's when I started working with Mack Muramaker and them. I was in the town playing around. Tallahassee and Quincy and, um, Panama City, Florida. Appalachicola.…

176.t: On the road with Ida Cox
176.s: About twelve years earlier Billie went on the road with Ida Cox, picking up musicians near Biloxi.
176.q: I was on the road with Ida about, when long Papa been dead? How long look like I been dead? Oh, I can't hear. How long, honey, old man been dead? About ten years? About ten years. About twelve years ago I was on the road with Ida. About twelve years ago. Yeah, yeah, yeah. About twelve years ago.…

176.t: De De's trip toward Mexico while in Texas
176.s: De De says he never reached California but was heading to Mexico when his band split in Fort Worth after an uncle died in a Mexican mine.
176.q: He was in the mine, kind of mining operations like mining, you know, silver mine I believe in Mexico.

18.t: Hard times on the road and lodging
18.s: Small towns offer poor lodging; he always knew a woman in each town.
18.ch: Russell and Armstrong years, Goodman and the road
18.q: Some of the places you go you can't get no place to stay, in these smaller towns, you know. Someone will say, "Well, you go to Miss Jones and she'll rent you a room," or something like that. It's better than nothing, so you just have to put up with it and go along with it.

18.t: One-nighters, the private bus and weekly pay
18.s: They toured everywhere on a private bus on weekly pay with itineraries made by Henderson's agent.
18.ch: Cincinnati, Buffalo, Russell and Fletcher Henderson
18.q: Yeah. ... When we'd leave New York Fletcher's agent would have all these routines made out where we were going to play. We would make a copy so we would know where to write our chicks telling them what time to meet us...

18.t: George Washington and touring with Lucky Millinder
18.s: George Washington was a clown in Millinder's band; they traveled by bus for over a year.
18.ch: Russell and Armstrong years, Goodman and the road
18.q: By bus, yeah. And we got through the Holland Tunnel ... he got out the bus and kissed the ground. He had been traveling so much.

18.t: Cuthbert, Georgia: Fletcher Henderson's home town
18.s: The band visited Henderson's family in Cuthbert, where his father headed the school.
18.ch: Russell and Armstrong years, Goodman and the road
18.q: No. It's kind of tough, you know, you just don't. One place was Fletcher Henderson's home. (His father was [mayor?] and everything else down there.)

18.t: Touring with Helvey: Charleston, Dallas and Adolphus Trent
18.s: Helvey's band traveled widely; he met Margaret in Charleston and heard Adolphus Trent's band in Dallas.
18.ch: Cincinnati, Buffalo, Russell and Fletcher Henderson
18.q: We played all over... That's where I met my wife, down in Charleston. We played down in Charleston, that's where I met her.

149.t: What road life was really like
149.s: Goines and Hawkins discuss tiredness, a late dance in Bluefield and failing brakes.
149.q: We've had our tough times out there. But, you know, when you think about them, you say it's pretty rough through the years, but there were some very good experiences, the way things are today. You know, I say that kids don't know what they missed. But, I don't think they'd want to go through that.…

149.t: Bus breakdown on the Pennsylvania road
149.s: The band's bus broke down on a two-lane road in winter.
149.q: Well, one time I was on a tour before the turnpike was completed, like the Pennsylvania Turnpike, and we had to go from New York to Pittsburgh. I think that's one of the things I would change. Me riding in that bus with the whole band and it's this time of year. And, the bus broke down. And we had…

149.t: Driving the Caddy and the bus driver who taught him
149.s: He likes to drive, and recalls driver Ed Fitzgerald on the Dallas dash.
149.ch: Compositions, singers and the end of the big band
149.q: No. I get on pretty good. If I got time to make it, and I've got to go, I'll get in the Caddy. If I don't have that much time, then whatever need, I'll do.

149.s: He took the Ink Spots on tour for $75 each before 'If I Didn't Care' was a hit.
149.ch: Highlights, the reunion album and fellow musicians
149.q: Chicago. I went in with the Ink Spots for about 20 weeks tour. We played 20 weeks of nothing but theaters all over the country.

149.s: He played schools, dances and theaters in the South, with tours of 61 one-nighters.
149.q: lot of schools and all that. Besides dances and theaters, the ones that had theaters, I did quite a bit of touring. I remember touring there with Roy Hamilton 61 one-nighters after playing 18 one-nighters straight with Nat Cole. I jumped from one to the other. That's a lot of one nighters.

248.t: The Pelican band on the road by train in the country
248.s: The band worked mostly out of town, in Lacombe, Lake Charles, Shreveport and elsewhere, travelling by Southern Pacific train on a deal Clem had with the conductor.
248.ch: Booker T, the brass bands and the Pelican band
248.q: Emile O'Reilly played. Often on, they didn't have, you know, they had different guitar players. Sometimes he couldn't have a regular guitar player. After you know, they played, they didn't be playing spot jobs would it, you know? Yeah. But they had, he used Emile O'Reilly most of the time. Now that…

248.t: Pelican band on the road; Robichaux's country band
248.s: Dawson says he played mostly with Dusen and Clem's Pelican band, on the road all week, and that Robichaux's reading band also toured the country.
248.ch: Learning, lawn parties and band rivalries
248.q: No. He had his own line up. I never, I never played with him. I played more with Frankie Deucing, with, uh, Edward Clemmen, them, with that Pelican band. I played a long time with them. They kept, they, uh, they played, they used to go up in the country.

248.t: Trip to Indianapolis with George Jones for the Shriners
248.s: The band played the Claypool Hotel for several nights; Dawson declined an offer to stay, staying near home.
248.q: made a trip to indianapolis with him remember that that was a long time yeah i went with him we played for the shrines the white shrines that time they had the panama limit we left here i think it on a sunday morning around 11 o'clock and we got in indianapolis about two o'clock i mean about yes…

248.s: Dawson went with Jones's band to Indianapolis via Memphis in costume, expenses paid, with his tenor banjo a novelty there.
248.ch: Billy Phillips, George Jones and the Shriners trip
248.q: Went with the shrines. I went to Indianapolis with him. I took my tenor banjo that, uh, when I, when I went up there, there people were surprised. They had never seen him, had never seen a tenor banjo up there before. Yeah? Oh. And, uh, I, uh, he had, he had this, this fellow called Snow on the…

14.t: Monroe Boost Club sign and days in New Orleans
14.s: In New Orleans Love ties a man's necktie for a tip, hangs the Monroe Boost Club sign on the coach, and the band practices in the baggage car while Frankie Dusen, Peter Bocage and others visit.
14.ch: Train trip with the rich sponsors
14.q: I said, all right. Say, I guess you boys, we won't see y'all until the head report up at the Greenwald Hotel, used to call the roads at the Greenwald. Report every morning because they didn't know exactly when they'd leave, you see. They didn't want us to get mixed up. So, I come out on the…

14.t: Booking agent Mr. Lyons and the Wisconsin tour; syndicate plot
14.s: The band reaches St. Paul and Chippewa Falls, tours Wisconsin dance halls, and learns some boys want to form a smaller band.
14.q: We went on up and after we got up there, we got to St. Paul, Minnesota. We didn't give them no dance there, we went right on in the Chippewa 4. We stopped at the Ottawa Hotel. And the whole time we were there, about two or three days we rehearsed, you know. And the booking agent lived in that town,…

14.t: Sleeping in the baggage car, Baton Rouge dance and payoff
14.s: The band sleeps on cots in the baggage car, wakes up back in Alexandria, stops two days in Baton Rouge to play a dance, and is paid off in Monroe.
14.ch: Train trip with the rich sponsors
14.q: Man, I made so much money. Dr. William give us $20 a piece to have fun with. I didn't know what to do with money then. I just put pocket that money in. I had some fun, but I didn't know nothing about spending no big money then. So we had a time. Frankie and all of them come down and enjoyed…

14.t: Lost Mexico City job; Howard Walker's bus band leaves for Minnesota
14.s: A $20-a-night Mexico City job collapses when the track is blown up; back home, Howard Walker rehearses a band two weeks and heads north, playing dances along the way.
14.q: They're good musicians and they got the music ranged up. Were you ready? Towards last, yeah. Towards last they had got a good job before they blew up that track there. We were going to Mexico City. I had done practiced up with the band. They had a good job there. Twenty dollars a night, all expense…

303.t: One-night stands in Texas with his own band
303.s: Riddick lists Texas towns played on one-night stands with his own band and names sidemen such as Tony Fougerat, Harry Shields and Charlie DuPont.

303.t: Hotels on the road and Billy Neuberger

303.ch: Hotel bands, Texas friends and the scrapbook

303.t: Staying in private homes; Atmore, Alabama 1926

107.t: Life on the road by bus
107.s: He enjoyed the road and bus travel until years later.
107.q: Mostly bus at the time. There was some air travel, but mostly the bus. And I didn’t fall out of love with the bus until years later.

400.t: Calloway's private train car, dignity and punctuality

400.t: Theater tours by Pullman with Cab's baggage car and green Lincoln
400.s: After the Cotton Club the band toured vaudeville theaters coast to coast by Pullman, with a baggage car holding trunks and Cab's green Lincoln.
400.ch: Cab Calloway's band: road, arrangers and shows
400.q: One Sweet [Unintelligible], all those great things. So that was the era. Traveling is what I want to get back to. We had six months in the Cotton Club, then we started… after the Cotton Club the next group would come in, Duke Ellington and Ethel Waters would be next, something like that. And we…

400.s: Hinton learned from the Missourians where to stay and eat; black hotels overcharged and were awful, one owner charging two prices for two sleeps.
